notes.overview: This chapter studies how light behaves when it bounces off surfaces (reflection) and when it passes from one transparent medium into another (refraction), covering spherical mirrors and lenses, the formulas that describe image formation, and everyday applications such as vehicle mirrors and corrective eyeglasses.

sections.title: 1. Reflection of Light and Spherical Mirrors
sections.content: The laws of reflection state that the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane; these laws hold for all reflecting surfaces, including curved ones. A spherical mirror is a mirror whose reflecting surface is a part of a hollow sphere: a concave mirror has its reflecting surface curved inward (towards the centre of the sphere), while a convex mirror has its reflecting surface curved outward. Key terms include the pole (centre of the mirror's surface), centre of curvature (centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part), radius of curvature, principal axis, and principal focus (the point on the axis where rays parallel to the axis converge, or appear to diverge from, after reflection).

sections.title: 2. Image Formation by Concave and Convex Mirrors
sections.content: A concave mirror can form both real and inverted images, or virtual and erect images, depending on the position of the object: an object placed beyond the centre of curvature forms a real, inverted, diminished image between the focus and centre of curvature, while an object placed between the pole and focus forms a virtual, erect, magnified image behind the mirror, which is why concave mirrors are used as shaving mirrors when held close to the face. A convex mirror, in contrast, always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image, irrespective of the object's distance, between the pole and focus, for any position of the object.
sections.video_title: Image Formation by a Concave Mirror (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 3. Mirror Formula, Magnification and Sign Convention
sections.content: The mirror formula relates the object distance (u), image distance (v) and focal length (f) of a spherical mirror: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. The linear magnification (m) produced by a spherical mirror is the ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object, and is also related to the object and image distances: m = h'/h = -v/u. According to the New Cartesian Sign Convention, all distances are measured from the pole of the mirror, distances measured in the direction of the incident ray (to the right) are taken as positive, and those against it (to the left) are negative; heights measured upwards are positive, downwards are negative.
sections.video_title: Mirror Formula, Magnification & Sign Convention (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 4. Uses of Spherical Mirrors
sections.content: Concave mirrors are commonly used in torches, search-lights and vehicle headlights to get powerful parallel beams of light by placing the light source at their focus; they are also used as shaving mirrors to see a larger image of the face, and by dentists to obtain a magnified image of teeth. Convex mirrors are used as rear-view (side) mirrors in vehicles because they always give an erect, though diminished, image and have a much wider field of view, allowing the driver to see most of the traffic behind.

sections.title: 5. Refraction of Light
sections.content: Refraction is the change in direction of light as it passes obliquely from one transparent medium to another, caused by a change in the speed of light in the two media - light bends towards the normal when entering a denser medium and away from the normal when entering a rarer medium, while light travelling along the normal passes without bending. The laws of refraction state that the incident ray, refracted ray and normal all lie in the same plane, and the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant for a given pair of media (Snell's Law).

sections.title: 6. Refractive Index
sections.content: The refractive index of a medium is a measure of how much it bends light, defined as the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum (or air) to the speed of light in that medium; a higher refractive index means light bends more and travels more slowly in that medium. When light travels from a rarer medium (like air) into a denser medium (like glass or water), it slows down and bends towards the normal; when going from denser to rarer, it speeds up and bends away from the normal.

sections.title: 7. Refraction by Spherical Lenses
sections.content: A lens is a transparent material bound by two surfaces, of which at least one is curved. A convex (converging) lens is thicker at the middle than at the edges and converges a parallel beam of light to a point (the principal focus) after refraction, while a concave (diverging) lens is thinner at the middle and diverges a parallel beam of light, appearing to come from a point on the same side as the incident beam. Key terms include optical centre, principal axis, and the two principal foci on either side of the lens.

sections.title: 8. Image Formation by Lenses; Lens Formula and Magnification
sections.content: A convex lens forms different types of images depending on the object's position: a real, inverted image (diminished, same size, or magnified depending on distance) when the object is beyond the focus, and a virtual, erect, magnified image when the object is between the optical centre and focus (used in magnifying glasses). A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image, regardless of the object's position. The lens formula relates object distance, image distance and focal length: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f, and magnification is given by m = h'/h = v/u.
sections.video_title: Formation of Images by a Convex Lens (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 9. Power of a Lens
sections.content: The power of a lens is defined as the reciprocal of its focal length (in metres), P = 1/f, and is measured in dioptres (D); a convex (converging) lens has positive power, while a concave (diverging) lens has negative power. Opticians prescribe corrective lenses in terms of power - for example, a combination of lenses is used in corrective eyeglasses, cameras and microscopes, and the total power of two thin lenses held in contact is the sum of their individual powers.

key_terms.Pole: The centre point of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror.
key_terms.Focal length: The distance between the pole and the principal focus of a spherical mirror or lens.
key_terms.Refractive index: The ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in a given medium; a measure of how much a medium bends light.
key_terms.Power of a lens: The reciprocal of the focal length (in metres), measured in dioptres, indicating how strongly a lens converges or diverges light.
key_terms.Magnification: The ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object, indicating how much larger or smaller the image is.

important_facts: Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f
Lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f
Power of lens: P = 1/f (metres), unit dioptre (D)
Convex mirrors and concave lenses always form virtual, erect, diminished images.
Refractive index of a denser medium is higher; light travels slower in a denser medium.
exam_tips: Practice ray diagrams for concave and convex mirrors/lenses for different object positions - a very common 3 or 5 mark question.
Be careful with the sign convention when substituting values into the mirror/lens formula.
Learn the everyday uses of concave/convex mirrors and lenses, as these appear frequently as 1-2 mark questions.

questions.question: A mirror that always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image is a:
questions.explanation: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image regardless of object position.

questions.question: When light travels from air into glass, it:
options: Speeds up and bends away from normal
Slows down and bends towards normal
Speeds up and bends towards normal
Travels at the same speed with no bending
questions.explanation: Glass is denser than air, so light slows down and bends towards the normal.

questions.question: The power of a convex lens of focal length 50 cm is:
questions.explanation: P = 1/f = 1/0.5 m = +2 D (positive since convex lens).

questions.question: Vehicles use convex mirrors as rear-view mirrors mainly because they:
options: Have a wider field of view
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors give a wider field of view, helping drivers see more of the traffic behind.

questions.question: A concave lens always forms an image that is:
questions.explanation: A concave (diverging) lens always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image.

questions.question: State the laws of reflection of light.

rubric.point: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection
Incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane

questions.model_answer: The angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.

questions.question: Define refractive index of a medium. What does a higher refractive index indicate?

rubric.point: Ratio of speed of light in vacuum/air to speed of light in the medium
Higher refractive index means light travels slower and bends more in that medium

questions.model_answer: The refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum (or air) to the speed of light in that medium. A higher refractive index indicates that light travels more slowly and bends more when entering that medium.

questions.question: Describe the nature, position and size of the image formed by a convex lens when the object is placed beyond the centre of curvature (2F1).

rubric.point: Image is real and inverted
Image is formed between F2 and 2F2 on the other side
Image is diminished (smaller than the object)

questions.model_answer: When an object is placed beyond 2F1 (beyond twice the focal length) of a convex lens, the image formed is real and inverted, located between F2 and 2F2 on the other side of the lens, and is diminished in size compared to the object.

questions.question: Give three uses of concave mirrors in daily life, explaining the reason for each use.

rubric.point: Used in torches/headlights/search-lights to produce powerful parallel beams (object placed at focus)
Used as shaving mirrors to see a large, erect image of the face (object placed close, within focus)
Used by doctors/dentists as head mirrors/examination mirrors to focus light and get a magnified view

questions.model_answer: Concave mirrors are used in torches, search-lights and vehicle headlights to produce powerful parallel beams of light, since a source placed at the focus produces a parallel reflected beam. They are used as shaving mirrors because, when held close to the face, they produce a large, erect and magnified image. They are also used by doctors and dentists as examination mirrors to focus light on a small area and obtain a magnified view.

questions.question: State the mirror formula and the sign convention used for spherical mirrors. Using ray diagrams, describe the image formed by a concave mirror when the object is placed (a) at the centre of curvature and (b) between the pole and the focus.

rubric.point: Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, relating object distance, image distance and focal length
Sign convention: distances measured from the pole; distances in the direction of incident light are positive, against it are negative
At centre of curvature: image is real, inverted, same size, formed at C itself
Between pole and focus: image is virtual, erect, magnified, formed behind the mirror
Ray diagram reasoning uses standard rays (parallel to axis reflecting through focus, through centre of curvature reflecting back on itself, through focus reflecting parallel to axis)

questions.model_answer: The mirror formula is 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, where u is the object distance, v is the image distance and f is the focal length. By the New Cartesian Sign Convention, all distances are measured from the pole of the mirror, with distances measured in the direction of the incident light taken as positive and those measured against it as negative. When an object is placed at the centre of curvature (C) of a concave mirror, the image formed is real, inverted, of the same size as the object, and is also formed at C. When the object is placed between the pole and the focus, the image formed is virtual, erect, magnified, and appears behind the mirror. These can be verified using ray diagrams drawn with standard rays: a ray parallel to the principal axis that reflects through the focus, a ray through the centre of curvature that reflects back along its own path, and a ray through the focus that reflects parallel to the principal axis.

questions.question: The point on the principal axis of a concave mirror where rays parallel to the axis converge after reflection is called the:
questions.explanation: Rays parallel to the principal axis converge at (or appear to diverge from) the principal focus after reflection.

questions.question: An object is placed between the pole and the focus of a concave mirror. The image formed is:
questions.explanation: When the object lies between the pole and focus of a concave mirror, the image formed is virtual, erect and magnified, behind the mirror.

questions.question: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. The image is formed at a distance of:
questions.explanation: Using 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with u=-30 cm, f=-10 cm: 1/v = -1/10 + 1/30 = -1/15, so v = -15 cm, i.e. a real image 15 cm from the mirror.

questions.question: In the New Cartesian Sign Convention for spherical mirrors, distances measured against the direction of the incident light are taken as:
questions.explanation: Distances measured against the direction of the incident ray (to the left of the pole) are taken as negative.

questions.question: Dentists use ___ mirrors to obtain a magnified view of a patient's teeth.
questions.explanation: Concave mirrors, held close to the teeth, form a magnified virtual image, which dentists use for examination.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the laws of refraction of light?
options: The incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in the same plane
The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of refraction
The ratio of sin(angle of incidence) to sin(angle of refraction) is constant for a given pair of media
This constant ratio is called the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first
questions.explanation: The angle of incidence being equal to the angle of reflection is a law of reflection, not refraction; in refraction the angles are generally different, related by Snell's law.

questions.question: A ray of light passes from water into air. On crossing the surface, it bends:
questions.explanation: Going from a denser medium (water) to a rarer medium (air), light speeds up and bends away from the normal.

questions.question: Light travels faster in medium A than in medium B. This means:
options: Medium A has a higher refractive index than medium B
Medium B has a higher refractive index than medium A
Both media have the same refractive index
Refractive index does not depend on the speed of light in the medium
questions.explanation: A lower speed of light corresponds to a higher refractive index, so medium B (where light is slower) has the higher refractive index.

questions.question: A lens that is thicker in the middle than at the edges is called a:
questions.explanation: A convex (converging) lens is thicker at the middle than at the edges.

questions.question: An object is placed 20 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. The image is formed at:
options: 20 cm on the other side, real, same size as the object
questions.explanation: Using 1/v - 1/u = 1/f with u=-20 cm, f=10 cm: 1/v = 1/10 - 1/20 = 1/20, so v=20 cm; since u=2f, the image is real, inverted and of the same size as the object.

questions.question: A simple magnifying glass is a convex lens used with the object placed:
options: Beyond 2F1, giving a real, diminished image
Between the optical centre and focus (F1), giving a virtual, erect, magnified image
At infinity, giving a real image at the focus
At 2F1, giving a real image of the same size
questions.explanation: When the object is between the optical centre and the focus of a convex lens, a virtual, erect and magnified image is formed, which is how a magnifying glass works.

questions.question: A lens has a power of -2.5 D. It is a:
options: Convex lens of focal length 40 cm
Concave lens of focal length 40 cm
Convex lens of focal length 25 cm
Concave lens of focal length 25 cm
questions.explanation: f = 1/P = 1/-2.5 = -0.4 m = -40 cm; the negative sign shows it is a concave (diverging) lens of focal length 40 cm.

questions.question: Two thin lenses of power +2 D and -1 D are held in contact. The power of the combination is:
questions.explanation: The net power of lenses in contact is the algebraic sum of their individual powers: +2 D + (-1 D) = +1 D.

questions.question: State the nature of the image formed by a convex mirror for an object at any distance, and explain why convex mirrors are preferred over plane mirrors as rear-view mirrors in vehicles.

rubric.point: Convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image irrespective of object position
Preferred because they give a wider field of view than a plane mirror of the same size

questions.model_answer: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image of an object, regardless of how far or near the object is placed. Convex mirrors are preferred over plane mirrors as rear-view mirrors because their curved surface gives a much wider field of view, allowing the driver to see a larger area of traffic behind the vehicle than a plane mirror of the same size would show.

questions.question: Define refraction of light. Why does a pencil partly immersed in water appear bent at the water surface?

rubric.point: Refraction is the change in direction of light as it passes obliquely from one medium to another due to a change in speed
Light rays from the immersed part bend (refract) at the water-air interface, so the eye perceives the image displaced, making the pencil appear bent

questions.model_answer: Refraction is the change in direction of light as it passes obliquely from one transparent medium to another, caused by a change in the speed of light between the two media. A pencil partly immersed in water appears bent because light rays coming from the submerged part of the pencil refract (bend) as they pass from water into air at the surface, so the eye traces them back along straight lines and perceives the submerged part as displaced, making the pencil look bent at the surface.

questions.question: Write the lens formula for a spherical lens, and state the sign convention used for measuring object distance and image distance.

rubric.point: Lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f
Distances measured from the optical centre; distances in the direction of incident light (towards the right) are positive, against it are negative

questions.model_answer: The lens formula is 1/v - 1/u = 1/f, where u is the object distance, v is the image distance, and f is the focal length. By convention, all distances are measured from the optical centre of the lens; distances measured in the direction of the incident light are taken as positive, and those measured against the direction of the incident light are taken as negative.

questions.question: Define the power of a lens and state its SI unit. An optician prescribes spectacles of power -2 D for a patient. What type of lens is required, and why?

rubric.point: Power is the reciprocal of focal length in metres, P=1/f, SI unit dioptre (D)
Negative power means a concave (diverging) lens is required, since concave lenses have negative power

questions.model_answer: The power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length measured in metres, P = 1/f, and its SI unit is the dioptre (D). Since the prescribed power is -2 D, a concave (diverging) lens of focal length 0.5 m is required, because concave lenses always have negative power, unlike convex lenses which have positive power.

questions.question: An object 4 cm high is placed 20 cm in front of a concave mirror, which forms a real image 8 cm high. Calculate the magnification produced and the image distance.

rubric.point: Magnification m = -h'/h = -8/4 = -2 (real, inverted, magnified twice)
Using m=-v/u: -2 = -v/-20, so v = -40 cm (image 40 cm in front of the mirror)

questions.model_answer: Since the image is real and inverted, magnification m = -h'/h = -8/4 = -2. Using m = -v/u with u = -20 cm: -2 = -v/(-20), which gives v = -40 cm. So the magnification is -2 (the image is twice the size of the object and inverted), and the image is formed 40 cm in front of the mirror.

questions.question: Describe the nature, position and size of the image formed by a concave mirror when the object is placed (a) at the focus, and (b) between the focus and the centre of curvature.

rubric.point: At the focus: image is formed at infinity, highly magnified, real and inverted
Between focus and centre of curvature: image is formed beyond the centre of curvature, real, inverted and magnified
In both cases the image is real and inverted, consistent with the object being at or beyond the focus

questions.model_answer: When an object is placed at the focus of a concave mirror, the reflected rays become parallel and the image is formed at infinity; it is highly magnified, real and inverted. When the object is placed between the focus and the centre of curvature, the image is formed beyond the centre of curvature, and is real, inverted and magnified. In both cases the image is real and inverted, since the object lies at or beyond the principal focus of the mirror.

questions.question: Define the refractive index of a medium in terms of the speed of light, and also express it in terms of the angle of incidence and angle of refraction. Calculate the refractive index of a medium in which the speed of light is 2x10^8 m/s (speed of light in vacuum = 3x10^8 m/s).

rubric.point: Refractive index n = speed of light in vacuum / speed of light in medium
Also n = sin(angle of incidence)/sin(angle of refraction) for a given pair of media (Snell's law)
Calculation: n = 3x10^8 / 2x10^8 = 1.5

questions.model_answer: The refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed of light in that medium, n = c/v. It can also be expressed, by Snell's law, as the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction for a given pair of media. Here, n = (3x10^8 m/s)/(2x10^8 m/s) = 1.5.

questions.question: State the nature, position and size of the image formed by a convex lens when the object is placed between the focus (F1) and twice the focal length (2F1).

rubric.point: Image is real and inverted
Image is formed beyond 2F2 on the other side of the lens
Image is magnified (larger than the object)

questions.model_answer: When an object is placed between the focus (F1) and 2F1 of a convex lens, the image formed is real and inverted, is located beyond 2F2 on the other side of the lens, and is magnified, i.e. larger than the object.

questions.question: With the help of a ray diagram, describe how a concave lens forms an image of an object placed at a finite distance in front of it. State two characteristics of this image.

rubric.point: A ray parallel to the principal axis appears, after refraction, to diverge from the focus on the same side as the object; a ray through the optical centre goes undeviated - their backward extensions meet to locate the image
The image is formed between the optical centre and the focus, on the same side as the object
The image is virtual, erect and diminished

questions.model_answer: For a concave lens, a ray of light travelling parallel to the principal axis, after refraction, appears to diverge from the focus on the same side of the lens as the object, while a ray passing through the optical centre goes straight without bending; tracing these two refracted rays backward, they appear to meet at a point between the optical centre and the focus, on the same side as the object, which locates the image. This image is virtual, erect and diminished in size compared to the object.

questions.question: Explain why the power of a combination of thin lenses held in contact is equal to the algebraic sum of their individual powers, and state one practical application of this idea.

rubric.point: For lenses in contact, the reciprocal of the combined focal length equals the sum of reciprocals of individual focal lengths: 1/F = 1/f1 + 1/f2 + ...
Since power P=1/f, this directly gives P = P1 + P2 + ... , the total power is the algebraic sum of individual powers
Application: opticians combine lenses to prescribe corrective eyeglasses of a required power, and in the design of cameras and microscopes

questions.model_answer: When thin lenses are held in contact, the reciprocal of the combined focal length equals the sum of the reciprocals of the individual focal lengths, 1/F = 1/f1 + 1/f2 + ...; since the power of a lens is defined as P = 1/f, this relation directly gives the total power of the combination as the algebraic sum of the individual powers, P = P1 + P2 + .... This principle is used by opticians to combine lenses of different powers to prescribe corrective eyeglasses of the exact power needed, and is also used in designing cameras and microscopes.

questions.topic: Lens formula, magnification and ray diagrams
questions.question: State the lens formula and the magnification formula for a spherical lens. Using ray diagrams, describe the nature, position and size of the image formed by a convex lens when the object is placed (a) beyond 2F1, and (b) between the optical centre and the focus (F1).

rubric.point: Lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f
Magnification: m = h'/h = v/u
Beyond 2F1: image is real, inverted and diminished, formed between F2 and 2F2 on the other side
Between optical centre and F1: image is virtual, erect and magnified, formed on the same side as the object (principle of magnifying glass)
Ray diagram reasoning uses standard rays: parallel to axis refracting through the focus, through the optical centre undeviated, and through the near focus emerging parallel to the axis

questions.model_answer: The lens formula is 1/v - 1/u = 1/f, and the magnification produced by a lens is m = h'/h = v/u. When an object is placed beyond 2F1 of a convex lens, the image formed is real, inverted and diminished, located between F2 and 2F2 on the other side of the lens. When the object is placed between the optical centre and the focus (F1), the image formed is virtual, erect and magnified, and appears on the same side of the lens as the object - this is the principle used in a magnifying glass. These images can be located using ray diagrams drawn with standard rays: a ray parallel to the principal axis that refracts through the focus on the far side, a ray through the optical centre that passes undeviated, and a ray through the near focus that emerges parallel to the principal axis after refraction.

questions.topic: Refraction, Snell's law and refractive index
questions.question: State the laws of refraction of light. Define refractive index and state its relation to the speed of light in a medium. Explain why a pencil partly immersed in water appears bent, and why a swimming pool appears shallower than its actual depth.

rubric.point: Laws of refraction: incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in the same plane; sin i / sin r is constant for a given pair of media
Refractive index n = speed of light in vacuum/air divided by speed of light in the medium
n is also equal to sin(angle of incidence)/sin(angle of refraction) for the given pair of media
Pencil appears bent because light from the submerged part refracts at the water-air surface, and the eye perceives the image along the refracted ray's apparent straight-line path
Pool appears shallower because light from the bottom bends away from the normal on leaving water, making the apparent depth less than the real depth

questions.model_answer: The laws of refraction state that the incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane, and that the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is constant for a given pair of media (Snell's law). The refractive index of a medium is defined as the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum (or air) to the speed of light in that medium, and by Snell's law it is also equal to sin(angle of incidence)/sin(angle of refraction) for that pair of media. A pencil partly immersed in water appears bent because light rays from the submerged part of the pencil bend (refract) as they pass from water into air at the surface; the eye traces these rays back along straight lines, so the submerged part appears displaced, making the pencil look bent at the surface. Similarly, a swimming pool appears shallower than it really is because light rays from the bottom of the pool bend away from the normal as they pass from water into air, making the apparent depth of the pool less than its real depth.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection, for any reflecting surface, plane or curved.
Reason (R): The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct laws of reflection, but R (about the rays lying in the same plane) does not explain why the two angles are equal - that is a separate, independent law.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A concave mirror always forms a real and inverted image.
Reason (R): When an object is placed between the pole and the focus of a concave mirror, the image formed is virtual and erect.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: A is false - a concave mirror forms a virtual, erect, magnified image when the object is between the pole and focus (e.g. as a shaving mirror). R correctly describes this case.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Convex mirrors are preferred over plane mirrors as vehicle rear-view mirrors.
Reason (R): A convex mirror always forms a diminished image, which allows it to cover a wider field of view than a plane mirror of the same size.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, and R correctly explains A: because the image is diminished, a larger area of the surroundings can be fitted into the mirror's field of view.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): In the New Cartesian Sign Convention, the focal length of a concave mirror is always taken as negative.
Reason (R): All distances are measured from the pole of the mirror, and distances measured against the direction of the incident light are taken as negative.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both are true. Since a concave mirror's focus lies in front of the mirror (against the direction of the incident ray, by convention), R correctly explains why its focal length is negative.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): When light travels from water into air, it bends away from the normal.
Reason (R): Air is optically denser than water.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: A is true - light does bend away from the normal going from water (denser) to air (rarer). But R is false: air is optically rarer than water, not denser.

questions.topic: Refractive index and speed of light
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Light travels more slowly in glass than in air.
Reason (R): Glass has a higher refractive index than air.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both are true, and R correctly explains A: a higher refractive index directly means light travels slower in that medium, since n = (speed in vacuum)/(speed in medium).

questions.question:
Assertion (A): For a given pair of media, the ratio sin(angle of incidence)/sin(angle of refraction) is the same for all angles of incidence.
Reason (R): This constant ratio is called the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true and together form Snell's law - R correctly identifies and explains the name of the constant ratio described in A.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A convex lens always forms a real and inverted image.
Reason (R): When an object is placed between the optical centre and the focus of a convex lens, the image formed is virtual, erect and magnified.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: A is false - a convex lens forms a virtual, erect, magnified image when the object is between the optical centre and focus (the magnifying-glass case). R correctly describes this.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A concave lens can never form a real image of a real object.
Reason (R): A concave lens always diverges an incident parallel beam of light, so the refracted rays never actually converge to a point.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both are true, and R correctly explains A: since a concave lens only diverges light, the refracted rays cannot meet to form a real image; they only appear to diverge from a virtual point.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A lens of power -4 D is a converging lens.
Reason (R): Concave lenses have negative power because their focal length is negative by the sign convention.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: A is false - negative power indicates a diverging (concave) lens, not a converging one. R is true and correctly explains why concave lenses have negative power.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A magnification of -2 produced by a mirror indicates a virtual, erect image twice the size of the object.
Reason (R): For spherical mirrors, a negative sign of magnification indicates a real and inverted image.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: A is false - a negative magnification for a mirror indicates a real, inverted image (a virtual, erect image always has positive magnification). R correctly states this rule.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The mirror formula (1/v + 1/u = 1/f) and the lens formula (1/v - 1/u = 1/f) have opposite signs before the 1/u term.
Reason (R): This is because mirrors and lenses use two completely different sign conventions for measuring object and image distances.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: A is true - the formulas do differ in sign. But R is false: both mirrors and lenses actually use the same New Cartesian Sign Convention; the difference in the formula arises from the geometry of reflection versus refraction, not from using different conventions.

questions.passage: Rohan, a Class 10 student, has been finding it difficult to read the blackboard from the back of his classroom, even though he can read a book held close to his eyes without any trouble. His eye doctor examined him and prescribed spectacles with a lens of power -2.5 D.

subquestions.question: What defect of vision is Rohan most likely suffering from?
subquestions.explanation: Difficulty seeing distant objects clearly while near objects remain clear is characteristic of myopia.

subquestions.question: What type of lens has been prescribed to correct this defect?
subquestions.explanation: The negative power (-2.5 D) indicates a concave (diverging) lens, used to correct myopia.

subquestions.question: Calculate the focal length of the prescribed lens, and briefly explain how a concave lens corrects Rohan's defect.

rubric.point: The concave lens diverges the incoming light slightly before it enters the eye, shifting the point of focus back onto the retina instead of in front of it

subquestions.model_answer: The focal length is f = 1/P = 1/(-2.5) = -0.4 m, i.e. -40 cm. In myopia, the eye lens focuses distant objects in front of the retina instead of on it. A concave lens diverges the incoming rays slightly before they reach the eye, which shifts the point of focus backward onto the retina, allowing Rohan to see distant objects clearly.

questions.passage: Meera wants to read the very fine print on a medicine label. She picks up a convex lens of focal length 5 cm, holds it close to the label at a distance of 3 cm, and looks through it.

subquestions.question: What kind of image will Meera see through the lens in this position?
subquestions.explanation: With the object between the optical centre and the focus of a convex lens, the image formed is virtual, erect and magnified.

subquestions.question: This use of a convex lens is the operating principle of which common device?
subquestions.explanation: Viewing a close object through a convex lens held within its focal length is exactly how a magnifying glass works.

subquestions.question: Using the lens formula, find the image distance for the label held 3 cm from the lens (f = 5 cm), and state whether this position is consistent with the magnifying-glass condition.

rubric.point: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f with u=-3, f=+5 gives 1/v = 1/5 - 1/3 = -2/15, so v = -7.5 cm (virtual image on the same side)
Since the object (3 cm) is within the focal length (5 cm), this matches the magnifying-glass condition, producing a virtual, magnified image

subquestions.model_answer: Using 1/v - 1/u = 1/f with u = -3 cm and f = +5 cm: 1/v = 1/5 + (-1/3) = -2/15, so v = -7.5 cm - a virtual image on the same side as the object. Since the label (3 cm) is placed within the lens's focal length (5 cm), this is exactly the condition needed for a magnifying glass, producing a virtual, erect, magnified image.

questions.passage: A car manufacturer compares a plane mirror and a curved mirror of the same size as options for the side rear-view mirror. Drivers using the curved mirror can see a noticeably larger area of the road behind them, though vehicles in the mirror look slightly smaller than they do in real life.

subquestions.question: Which type of spherical mirror is being used as the rear-view mirror?
subquestions.explanation: A mirror that gives a wider view with diminished images is a convex mirror.

subquestions.question: The image of vehicles seen in this mirror is:
subquestions.explanation: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image.

subquestions.question: Explain why a convex mirror gives a wider field of view than a plane mirror of the same size, and why manufacturers print 'Objects in mirror are closer than they appear' as a caution.

rubric.point: A convex mirror curves outward, so it can reflect light from a much larger area of the surroundings onto its surface compared to a flat mirror of the same size
Because the image is diminished, vehicles appear farther away than they really are, so the warning helps drivers correctly judge actual distance

subquestions.model_answer: A convex mirror's outward-curving surface allows it to reflect light rays from a much wider area of the surroundings than a flat mirror of the same size, giving it a wider field of view. However, because the image it forms is diminished, objects appear smaller and therefore seem farther away than they actually are - which is why manufacturers add the caution, so drivers correctly judge the real distance of vehicles behind them.

questions.passage: A torch has a small bulb placed in front of a curved reflecting surface inside its head. When the bulb is positioned at a certain special point on the mirror's principal axis, the torch produces a strong, parallel beam of light that travels a long distance without spreading out much.

subquestions.question: What type of mirror is used inside the torch?
subquestions.explanation: Concave mirrors are used in torches and headlights to produce strong parallel beams.

subquestions.question: At which point must the bulb be placed to produce a parallel beam?
subquestions.explanation: A point source placed at the principal focus of a concave mirror produces, after reflection, a beam parallel to the principal axis.

subquestions.question: Using the property of reflection at a concave mirror, explain why placing the bulb at this point produces a parallel beam instead of a spreading or converging one.

rubric.point: Any ray from a point source at the focus, after reflecting off a concave mirror, travels parallel to the principal axis - the reverse of the rule that rays parallel to the axis converge at the focus
Since all the reflected rays end up parallel to each other, the beam neither spreads out nor converges, letting it travel a long distance while staying concentrated

subquestions.model_answer: When a point source of light is placed exactly at the principal focus of a concave mirror, every ray from it, after reflecting off the mirror, travels parallel to the principal axis - this is simply the reverse of the rule that rays parallel to the axis converge at the focus. Because all the reflected rays end up parallel to one another, the resulting beam neither spreads out nor converges as it travels, allowing the torch to send a strong, concentrated beam over a long distance.

questions.passage: A teacher places a small, brightly-lit slide 15 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 10 cm inside a projector. The lens forms a large, inverted image of the slide on a screen placed far away, much bigger than the slide itself.

subquestions.question: For the projector lens to form a magnified real image on a distant screen, the slide (object) must be placed:
options: Between the optical centre and F1
subquestions.explanation: Placing the object between F1 and 2F1 of a convex lens produces a real, inverted, magnified image beyond 2F2 - exactly how a projector works.

subquestions.question: The image formed on the screen is:
subquestions.explanation: A convex lens with the object beyond F1 always forms a real, inverted image.

subquestions.question: Using the lens formula, find the image distance for the slide placed 15 cm from the lens (f = 10 cm), and state whether this is consistent with the object lying between F1 and 2F1.

rubric.point: Since 2F1 = 20 cm, the slide at 15 cm indeed lies between F1 (10 cm) and 2F1 (20 cm), consistent with a magnified real image forming beyond 2F2

subquestions.model_answer: Using 1/v - 1/u = 1/f with u = -15 cm and f = +10 cm: 1/v = 1/10 - 1/15 = 1/30, so v = +30 cm. Since 2F1 = 20 cm, the slide placed at 15 cm indeed lies between F1 (10 cm) and 2F1 (20 cm), which is consistent with the lens forming a real, inverted, magnified image well beyond 2F2, as seen on the projector screen.

questions.topic: Case study - lens combination in contact
questions.passage: In an optics lab, two thin lenses are held in close contact on the same stand: a convex lens of focal length 25 cm and a concave lens of focal length 50 cm.

subquestions.question: What is the power of the convex lens alone?
What is the power of the concave lens alone?
Find the power and equivalent focal length of the combination when both lenses are held in contact, and state whether the combination behaves overall as a converging or diverging system.

rubric.point: Total power P = P1 + P2 = +4 + (-2) = +2 D
Equivalent focal length F = 1/P = 1/2 = 0.5 m = 50 cm; since the net power is positive, the combination behaves as a converging (convex-like) system

subquestions.model_answer: The net power of lenses in contact is the algebraic sum of their individual powers: P = P1 + P2 = +4 D + (-2 D) = +2 D. The equivalent focal length is F = 1/P = 1/2 = 0.5 m, i.e. 50 cm. Since the combined power is positive, the combination behaves overall as a converging (convex-like) system.

questions.passage: A dentist uses a small mirror mounted on a long handle to examine a patient's teeth closely. When held very close to a tooth, the mirror produces a large, upright image of the tooth, making it easy to spot cavities.

subquestions.question: Which type of mirror does the dentist use, and why?
options: Convex mirror, for a wide field of view
Concave mirror, to get a magnified virtual image when held close
Plane mirror, for a true-to-size image
Convex mirror, to get a diminished image
subquestions.explanation: A concave mirror held close to an object gives a magnified virtual image, which is exactly what a dentist needs.

subquestions.question: For the mirror to produce this magnified, upright image, the tooth (object) must lie:
options: Between the pole and the focus
subquestions.explanation: A concave mirror forms a virtual, erect, magnified image only when the object is between the pole and the focus.

subquestions.question: Explain why this mirror position is essential for the dentist's purpose, and what would happen to the image if the mirror were moved further away so the tooth was beyond the focus.

rubric.point: Only when the object is between the pole and focus does a concave mirror produce a virtual, erect, magnified image, giving the dentist an enlarged, right-way-up view
If the tooth were beyond the focus, the image would become real and inverted, no longer giving the dentist a convenient upright, magnified view

subquestions.model_answer: A concave mirror only produces a virtual, erect, magnified image when the object is placed between the pole and the focus - this magnified, right-way-up view is essential for the dentist to clearly examine the tooth. If the mirror were moved further away so the tooth lay beyond the focus, the image would instead become real and inverted, which would no longer give the dentist a convenient upright, magnified view of the tooth.

questions.passage: A simple telescope uses a large convex lens (the objective lens) to collect light from a very distant star and form an image of it inside the telescope tube, which is then viewed through a second, smaller lens (the eyepiece).

subquestions.question: Since the star is an extremely distant object, where does the objective lens form its image?
options: Between the optical centre and the focus
subquestions.explanation: For an object at infinity, a convex lens forms the image exactly at its focus.

subquestions.question: The image formed by the objective lens of a very distant object is:
subquestions.explanation: An object at infinity forms a real, inverted, highly diminished image exactly at the focus.

subquestions.question: Explain why a convex lens, rather than a concave lens, must be used as the objective lens of a telescope, in terms of the kind of image each can form.

rubric.point: The telescope's objective must form a real image of the distant star so it can be further magnified and viewed through the eyepiece

A concave lens can never form a real image of a real object (it always forms a virtual image), so only a convex lens - which converges light to a real image at the focus - can work as the objective lens

subquestions.model_answer: A telescope's objective lens must form a real image of the distant star so that this image can be further magnified and viewed through the eyepiece. A concave lens can never form a real image of a real object - it only ever diverges light to form a virtual image - so only a convex lens, which converges light to form a real image at its focus, can serve as the telescope's objective lens.

questions.topic: Case study - concave mirror magnification numerical
questions.passage: In a physics lab activity, a student places a candle 4 cm tall at a distance of 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm, and catches a sharp, real image on a screen.

subquestions.question: Using the mirror formula, find the image distance (v).
What is the nature of the image formed?
subquestions.explanation: With v=-15 cm (real, in front of mirror) and |v|<|u|, the image is real, inverted and smaller than the object.

subquestions.question: Calculate the magnification produced and the height of the image.

rubric.point: Image height h' = m x h = -0.5 x 4 = -2 cm (2 cm tall, inverted)

subquestions.model_answer: Magnification m = -v/u = -(-15)/(-30) = -0.5. Image height h' = m x h = -0.5 x 4 cm = -2 cm, so the image is 2 cm tall and inverted (the negative sign confirming it is real and inverted), smaller than the 4 cm object.

questions.topic: Case study - combination of three lenses
questions.passage: An instrument designer combines three thin lenses in contact on the same axis: a convex lens of focal length 10 cm, a concave lens of focal length 20 cm, and a second convex lens of focal length 25 cm.

subquestions.question: What is the power of the first convex lens (f = 10 cm)?
What is the power of the concave lens (f = 20 cm)?
Given that the second convex lens (f = 25 cm) has a power of +4 D, find the total power and the equivalent focal length of all three lenses held together in contact.

rubric.point: Total power P = P1 + P2 + P3 = 10 + (-5) + 4 = +9 D
Equivalent focal length F = 1/P = 1/9 m, approximately 11.1 cm; since power is positive, the combination is converging

subquestions.model_answer: For any number of thin lenses in contact, the rule extends directly: total power is the algebraic sum of all individual powers, P = P1 + P2 + P3 = (+10) + (-5) + (+4) = +9 D. The equivalent focal length is F = 1/P = 1/9 m ≈ 0.111 m, i.e. about 11.1 cm. Since the net power is positive, the three-lens combination behaves overall as a converging system, just as with two lenses.

questions.topic: Concave mirror image position for enlarged virtual image
questions.question: When an object was kept at position X in front of a concave mirror, an enlarged and virtual image was formed. Which among the following identifies X correctly?
options: Anywhere between the centre of curvature and principal focus
Anywhere between the pole and principal focus
Exactly at the centre of curvature
questions.explanation: A concave mirror gives an enlarged, virtual, erect image only when the object is placed between the pole and the focus (e.g. as a shaving mirror).

questions.topic: Search mirrors - convex mirror field of view
questions.question: Search mirrors are mirrors used to look for hidden objects underneath cars, and provide a wider field of view than a plane mirror. (a) What type of mirror is generally used to make search mirrors? (b) Describe the nature of the image formed by this type of mirror.

rubric.point: A convex mirror is used
The image formed is virtual, erect and diminished

questions.model_answer: A convex mirror is used to make search mirrors. A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image of an object placed in front of it, for any position of the object, and its diverging surface gives it a wider field of view than a plane mirror of the same size - which is why it can reveal hidden objects underneath a car.

questions.topic: Refractive index and speed of light - numerical
questions.question: The absolute refractive indices of two media P and Q are 1.33 and 2.52 respectively. The speed of light in medium P is 2 x 10^8 m/s. (a) What is the speed of light in medium Q? (b) If the angle of incidence for a ray of light travelling from medium P to Q is 0 degrees, what will be the path of light in medium Q?

rubric.point: At 0 degrees angle of incidence, the ray travels along the normal and passes undeviated into medium Q

questions.model_answer: Since nP/nQ = vQ/vP, vQ = (nP x vP)/nQ = (1.33 x 2x10^8)/2.52 = 1.056 x 10^8 m/s. Since the angle of incidence is 0 degrees, the ray of light is travelling along the normal, so it passes into medium Q without any bending - it continues undeviated in a straight line.

questions.topic: Dispersion of white light through prisms
questions.question: A beam of white light is passed through a series of three identical equilateral prisms placed one after another, such that the beam that emerges from Prism 1 enters Prism 2, and so on, finally falling on a screen after emerging from Prism 3. (a) What colour(s) will be seen on the screen? (b) Describe how the beam of light travels through the three prisms, from entering Prism 1 to emerging from Prism 3 and falling on the screen. (c) Name all the optical processes that take place as the beam of light enters Prism 1 and emerges from Prism 3.

rubric.point: A single prism splits white light into the seven VIBGYOR colours (violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red) by dispersion
A second identical prism placed to intercept the dispersed beam, oriented appropriately, recombines the spectrum back into white light
So the beam entering Prism 1 disperses into the spectrum, Prism 2 recombines it back to white light, and Prism 3 disperses it into the spectrum again - so the screen shows the VIBGYOR spectrum
The two processes involved are refraction (bending of light at each prism surface) and dispersion (splitting into constituent colours, since each colour refracts by a different amount)

questions.model_answer: The first prism disperses the white light into its seven constituent colours (VIBGYOR - violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red), since each colour of light refracts by a slightly different amount as it passes through the prism (violet bending the most, red the least). If the second prism is placed to intercept this dispersed beam in the reverse orientation, it recombines the spectrum back into white light. This white light then enters the third prism, which disperses it into the spectrum once again - so the screen finally shows the VIBGYOR spectrum. The processes taking place throughout are refraction (the bending of light at each prism surface) and dispersion (the splitting of white light into its constituent colours due to their different refractive indices in glass).

notes.overview: This chapter covers electric current and circuits, the relationship between potential difference, current and resistance (Ohm's Law), how resistors combine in series and parallel, and the heating and power effects of electric current, which underpin how household electrical appliances and wiring work.

sections.title: 1. Electric Current and Circuit
sections.content: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor, defined as current I = Q/t, where Q is the charge (in coulombs) and t is time (in seconds); its SI unit is the ampere (A), and it is conventionally taken to flow in the direction of positive charge flow (opposite to actual electron flow in a metallic conductor). An electric circuit is a continuous closed path along which electric current flows, typically consisting of a source (cell/battery), connecting wires, a switch, and a device such as a bulb or resistor; an ammeter measures current and is always connected in series in a circuit.

sections.title: 2. Electric Potential and Potential Difference
sections.content: The electric potential difference between two points in a circuit is the work done to move a unit charge from one point to another, given by V = W/Q, measured in volts (V); one volt is the potential difference when one joule of work is done to move one coulomb of charge. A voltmeter measures potential difference and is always connected in parallel across the component whose potential difference is to be measured. A cell or battery maintains the potential difference across a circuit by doing work on charges to drive the current.

sections.title: 3. Ohm's Law
sections.content: Ohm's Law states that the potential difference across the ends of a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the current flowing through it, provided the temperature remains constant: V is proportional to I, or V = IR, where R is the resistance of the conductor, measured in ohms (symbol omega). Resistance is the property of a conductor that opposes the flow of current through it; a graph of V versus I for an ohmic conductor is a straight line passing through the origin, with slope equal to the resistance.

sections.title: 4. Factors Affecting Resistance; Resistivity
sections.content: The resistance of a conductor depends on its length (directly proportional - longer wires have more resistance), its area of cross-section (inversely proportional - thicker wires have less resistance), and the nature of the material, expressed through the formula R = (rho x L)/A, where rho (resistivity) is a characteristic property of the material, measured in ohm-metre. Resistivity depends only on the material and temperature, not on the dimensions of the conductor; alloys like nichrome have high resistivity and are used in heating elements because they do not oxidise readily at high temperatures.
sections.video_title: Factors Affecting Resistance of a Conductor (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 5. Resistors in Series
sections.content: When resistors are connected end-to-end so that the same current flows through each of them, they are said to be connected in series; the total (equivalent) resistance is the sum of the individual resistances: Rs = R1 + R2 + R3. In a series combination, the current through each resistor is the same, but the potential difference is divided among the resistors in proportion to their resistance, and the equivalent resistance is always greater than the largest individual resistance.
sections.video_title: Resistance of a System of Resistors - Series (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 6. Resistors in Parallel
sections.content: When resistors are connected between the same two points, so that the potential difference across each is the same, they are said to be connected in parallel; the reciprocal of the total (equivalent) resistance is the sum of the reciprocals of individual resistances: 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. In a parallel combination, the potential difference across each resistor is the same, but the current divides among the branches, and the equivalent resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance - household circuits are wired in parallel so that each appliance gets the same voltage and can be switched independently.

sections.title: 7. Heating Effect of Electric Current
sections.content: When an electric current flows through a purely resistive conductor, electrical energy is dissipated entirely as heat, a phenomenon called the heating effect of current, quantified by Joule's law of heating: H = I^2 x R x t, where H is the heat produced, I is the current, R is the resistance, and t is the time for which the current flows. This effect is put to practical use in devices such as electric heaters, irons and toasters, which use nichrome heating elements, but is an undesirable loss of energy in devices like motors and generators, and is also the underlying principle of a fuse, which protects circuits from excessive current.

sections.title: 8. Electric Power and Commercial Units of Energy
sections.content: Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed or work is done, given by P = VI, and can also be expressed as P = I^2R or P = V^2/R, measured in watts (W); a device rated 'X watts, Y volts' indicates the power it consumes when operated at the stated voltage. The commercial unit of electrical energy is the kilowatt-hour (kWh), commonly called a 'unit' of electricity, where 1 kWh is the energy consumed by a 1000-watt appliance operating for 1 hour, and electricity bills are calculated based on the number of units (kWh) consumed.

key_terms.Electric current: The rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor, measured in amperes.
key_terms.Potential difference: The work done per unit charge to move it between two points, measured in volts.
key_terms.Resistance: The opposition offered by a conductor to the flow of current, measured in ohms.
key_terms.Resistivity: A material-dependent property that determines resistance per unit length and cross-sectional area.
key_terms.Kilowatt-hour: The commercial unit of electrical energy; the energy consumed by a 1000-watt device operating for 1 hour.

important_facts: Ohm's Law: V = IR
Series resistance: Rs = R1 + R2 + R3 (always greater than the largest resistor)
Parallel resistance: 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 (always less than the smallest resistor)
Joule's Law of heating: H = I^2Rt
1 kWh (1 unit) = energy used by a 1000 W appliance in 1 hour = 3.6 x 10^6 joules
exam_tips: Practice numerical problems using V=IR, series/parallel resistance formulas, and P=VI - these are frequently 3 or 5 mark questions.
Remember ammeters go in series and voltmeters go in parallel - a common conceptual MCQ/2-mark question.
Be clear on why household circuits use parallel wiring rather than series wiring.

questions.question: According to Ohm's Law, V equals:
questions.explanation: Ohm's Law states V = IR.

questions.question: In a series circuit, the current through each resistor is:
options: Dependent only on the largest resistor
questions.explanation: In series, the same current flows through all components.

questions.explanation: A voltmeter is connected in parallel to measure potential difference across a component.

questions.question: The resistance of a conductor is inversely proportional to its:
questions.explanation: Resistance is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section (R = rho L/A).

questions.question: One unit of electricity (as billed) equals:

questions.question: State Ohm's Law and write the formula relating V, I and R.

rubric.point: Potential difference across a conductor is directly proportional to current, at constant temperature
Formula: V = IR

questions.model_answer: Ohm's Law states that the potential difference across the ends of a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the current flowing through it, provided the temperature remains constant. This is expressed as V = IR, where R is the resistance of the conductor.

questions.question: State Joule's law of heating.

rubric.point: Heat produced is proportional to the square of the current
Also proportional to resistance and time: H = I^2Rt

questions.model_answer: Joule's law of heating states that the heat produced in a resistor is directly proportional to the square of the current passing through it, directly proportional to the resistance, and directly proportional to the time for which the current flows, expressed as H = I^2Rt.

questions.question: Give three differences between resistors connected in series and in parallel.

rubric.point: In series, current is the same through all resistors; in parallel, current divides among branches
In series, potential difference divides among resistors; in parallel, potential difference is the same across each
Equivalent resistance: series resistance is greater than the largest resistor; parallel resistance is less than the smallest resistor

questions.model_answer: In a series combination, the same current flows through each resistor, whereas in a parallel combination, the current divides among the different branches. In series, the total potential difference is divided among the resistors, whereas in parallel, the potential difference across each resistor is the same. The equivalent resistance in series is always greater than the largest individual resistance, while in parallel it is always less than the smallest individual resistance.

questions.question: Why are household electrical appliances connected in parallel rather than in series? Give three reasons.

rubric.point: Each appliance gets the same (full) voltage, so they work at their rated power regardless of others
Appliances can be switched on/off independently without affecting others
If one appliance is damaged or a fault occurs, other appliances are not affected and continue to work

questions.model_answer: Household appliances are connected in parallel because each appliance then receives the same voltage as the mains supply, allowing it to operate at its rated power regardless of other appliances. Parallel wiring also allows each appliance to be switched on or off independently without affecting the others. Additionally, if one appliance develops a fault or is damaged, the parallel arrangement ensures that the other appliances continue to function normally.

questions.question: Define resistance and state the factors on which the resistance of a conductor depends. Derive the expression for the equivalent resistance of resistors connected (a) in series and (b) in parallel.

rubric.point: Resistance is the opposition offered by a conductor to the flow of current, R = V/I
Depends on length (directly), area of cross-section (inversely), nature/resistivity of material, and temperature
Series: same current I through R1,R2,R3; total voltage V = V1+V2+V3 = I(R1+R2+R3), so Rs = R1+R2+R3
Parallel: same voltage V across R1,R2,R3; total current I = I1+I2+I3 = V(1/R1+1/R2+1/R3), so 1/Rp = 1/R1+1/R2+1/R3
Conclusion: series resistance adds up directly (larger), parallel resistance combines as reciprocals (smaller than smallest)

questions.model_answer: Resistance is the property of a conductor that opposes the flow of electric current through it, defined as R = V/I. It depends on the length of the conductor (directly proportional), its area of cross-section (inversely proportional), the nature of the material (resistivity), and its temperature. For resistors in series, the same current I flows through each resistor R1, R2 and R3, and the total voltage across the combination is the sum of the individual voltage drops: V = V1 + V2 + V3 = I R1 + I R2 + I R3 = I(R1+R2+R3), giving an equivalent resistance Rs = R1 + R2 + R3. For resistors in parallel, the voltage V across each resistor is the same, while the total current drawn is the sum of the currents through each branch: I = I1 + I2 + I3 = V/R1 + V/R2 + V/R3 = V(1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3), giving an equivalent resistance defined by 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. As a result, the equivalent resistance in series is always greater than the largest individual resistance, whereas in parallel it is always smaller than the smallest individual resistance.

questions.model_answer: An ammeter measures the current flowing in a circuit; it has a very low resistance and is always connected in series with the component so that the current is not altered. questions.question: On what factors does the resistivity of a material depend? Why is resistivity considered a more fundamental property of a material than resistance?

rubric.point: Resistivity depends only on the nature of the material and its temperature

questions.model_answer: Resistivity depends only on the nature of the material and its temperature, not on the dimensions of the conductor. Resistance, on the other hand, depends on both the resistivity of the material and the conductor's length and area of cross-section. questions.question: Two resistors of 5 ohm and 10 ohm are connected in series across a 15 V battery. Find the current flowing through the circuit.

questions.question: Describe how you would verify Ohm's law for a metallic conductor using a circuit with an ammeter, voltmeter and rheostat. What does the slope of the V-I graph represent?

Readings of V and I are taken for several settings and a graph of V versus I is plotted
The V-I graph is a straight line through the origin, and its slope equals the resistance R of the conductor

questions.model_answer: To verify Ohm's law, a metallic conductor is connected in a circuit with a battery, an ammeter in series to measure current, a voltmeter in parallel across the conductor to measure potential difference, and a rheostat to vary the current while keeping the temperature constant. For several different settings of the rheostat, the corresponding values of V and I are recorded, and a graph of V against I is plotted. questions.model_answer: Using R = rho L/A, with rho = 1.7x10^-8 ohm-m, L = 2 m and A = 1x10^-6 m^2: R = (1.7x10^-8 x 2)/(1x10^-6) = 3.4x10^-2 ohm = 0.034 ohm.

questions.question: A 2 ohm resistor is connected in series with a parallel combination of a 3 ohm and a 6 ohm resistor. Calculate the total resistance of the circuit.

questions.question: What is an electric fuse? Explain its working principle, and state why it must always be connected in series, never in parallel, in a circuit.

rubric.point: A fuse is a safety device consisting of a wire of a material with a low melting point that breaks the circuit if the current exceeds a safe value
It works on the heating effect of current (I^2R); excessive current heats the fuse wire until it melts and cuts off the supply
It must be in series so the entire circuit current passes through it and can be interrupted; in parallel it would carry only a fraction of the current and could not protect the circuit
keywords: parallel would not carry full current

questions.model_answer: An electric fuse is a safety device made of a wire of an alloy with a low melting point, connected in a circuit to protect it from excessive current. It works on the heating effect of current: if the current exceeds a safe value, the I^2R heating melts the fuse wire, breaking the circuit and stopping the current flow. A fuse must always be connected in series so that the entire circuit current flows through it, allowing it to sense and interrupt the total current; if connected in parallel, it would carry only a fraction of the current and would not be able to protect the rest of the circuit.

questions.topic: Ohm's law and factors affecting resistance
questions.question: State Ohm's law and describe, with a circuit diagram in words, how you would verify it experimentally. A wire of resistance 10 ohm is stretched uniformly to double its length. Assuming its volume remains constant, calculate its new resistance.

rubric.point: Ohm's law: V is directly proportional to I at constant temperature, V=IR
Experimental setup: cell/battery, ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel across the resistor, and a rheostat to vary the current
V-I graph obtained is a straight line through the origin, confirming Ohm's law; slope gives resistance
On stretching: length doubles and, since volume is constant, area of cross-section halves, and R=rho L/A
New resistance = original R x 2 x 2 = 4 x 10 = 40 ohm

questions.model_answer: Ohm's law states that the potential difference across a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the current flowing through it, provided the temperature remains constant, expressed as V = IR. To verify this, a conductor is connected in a circuit with a battery, an ammeter in series to measure current, a voltmeter in parallel across the conductor to measure potential difference, and a rheostat to vary the current. Readings of V and I are taken for several current values and plotted; the resulting V-I graph is a straight line through the origin, confirming Ohm's law, with the slope of the line giving the resistance. When the wire is stretched to double its length while its volume remains constant, its area of cross-section is halved. Since R = rho L/A, doubling L and halving A both increase resistance by a factor of 2, so the resistance increases by a factor of 2 x 2 = 4. The new resistance is therefore 4 x 10 = 40 ohm.

questions.question: Define electric power and derive expressions for it in terms of (i) V and I, (ii) I and R, and (iii) V and R. A household uses two 60 W bulbs and one 1000 W heater, each for 5 hours daily. Calculate the total energy consumed in kWh in 30 days, and the electricity bill if the cost is Rs 6 per unit.

rubric.point: Power is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed/work is done, P = W/t = VI
Substituting V=IR into P=VI gives P = I^2R; substituting I=V/R gives P = V^2/R
Energy for 30 days = 1.12 x 5 x 30 = 168 kWh
Bill = 168 x 6 = Rs 1008

questions.model_answer: Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed, P = W/t = VI. Substituting V = IR gives P = I^2R, and substituting I = V/R gives P = V^2/R. The total power consumed by the two 60 W bulbs and the 1000 W heater is 60+60+1000 = 1120 W = 1.12 kW. Used for 5 hours daily over 30 days, the total energy consumed is 1.12 x 5 x 30 = 168 kWh. At a cost of Rs 6 per unit (kWh), the electricity bill is 168 x 6 = Rs 1008.

questions.passage: A student connects a 5 ohm, an 8 ohm and a 12 ohm resistor in series with a 6 V battery, an ammeter and a switch to form a simple circuit.

subquestions.question: What is the total (equivalent) resistance of the circuit?

rubric.point: V(5)+V(8)+V(12) = 1.2+1.92+2.88 = 6 V, matching the battery voltage, confirming Kirchhoff's voltage rule for series circuits

subquestions.model_answer: The potential difference across the 8 ohm resistor is V = I x R = 0.24 x 8 = 1.92 V. Checking all three: V(5)=0.24x5=1.2V, V(8)=1.92V, V(12)=0.24x12=2.88V. Their sum is 1.2+1.92+2.88 = 6 V, exactly equal to the battery's 6 V, confirming that in a series circuit the individual potential drops add up to the total supplied voltage.

questions.passage: In a circuit, a 2 ohm resistor and a 4 ohm resistor are connected in parallel between points X and Y. An ammeter shows that a total current of 2 A flows into the parallel combination from the battery.

rubric.point: Current through 4 ohm branch = V/R = (8/3)/4 = 2/3 ≈ 0.67 A
This is consistent with the branches sharing the total 2 A in inverse proportion to their resistance (more current through the smaller 2 ohm resistor)

subquestions.model_answer: The current through the 4 ohm resistor is I = V/R = (8/3)/4 = 2/3 A ≈ 0.67 A. This makes sense because the total 2 A splits between the two branches in inverse proportion to their resistance - the smaller 2 ohm resistor carries the larger share (1.33 A) and the larger 4 ohm resistor carries the smaller share (0.67 A), together adding up to the total 2 A.

questions.passage: A circuit is built with a 6 ohm resistor in parallel with a 3 ohm resistor; this combination is then connected in series with a 4 ohm resistor and a 12 V battery.

The voltage across the parallel section is I x Rp = 2 x 2 = 4 V, so the current through the 3 ohm resistor is 4/3 ≈ 1.33 A (and correspondingly 4/6 ≈ 0.67 A flows through the 6 ohm resistor, together adding to the total 2 A).

questions.topic: Case study - wire stretching and resistance
questions.passage: A uniform wire has a resistance of 20 ohm. It is cut into two exactly equal halves, and the two halves are then connected together in parallel.

subquestions.question: What is the resistance of each half of the wire?
subquestions.explanation: Since resistance is proportional to length, halving the length halves the resistance: 20/2 = 10 ohm.

subquestions.question: When the two 10 ohm halves are connected in parallel, the equivalent resistance is:
Express the final equivalent resistance as a fraction of the original resistance R, and explain the general result in terms of R = rho L/A.

rubric.point: Final resistance (5 ohm) is R/4, one-quarter of the original 20 ohm
Cutting halves the length (L/2, halving resistance) and joining in parallel effectively doubles the area (halving resistance again), so R = rho L/A drops to a quarter overall

subquestions.model_answer: The final equivalent resistance (5 ohm) is exactly R/4, one-quarter of the original 20 ohm resistance. This can be understood through R = rho L/A: cutting the wire in half halves the length (which alone would halve the resistance), and recombining the two halves in parallel is equivalent to doubling the effective cross-sectional area (which alone would also halve the resistance) - together these two effects reduce the resistance to one-quarter of its original value.

subquestions.model_answer: The ratio of resistances is R(P):R(Q) = 806.7:484, approximately 5:3 - notice the lower-wattage lamp (P, 60 W) actually has the higher resistance. When connected in series, the same current flows through both lamps, so the power dissipated in each (P = I^2R) is greater in whichever has the higher resistance. This means lamp P, despite being rated for less power, will glow brighter than lamp Q in this series connection - the opposite of how they'd compare if each were run separately at its own rated 220 V.

questions.topic: Choosing the correct ammeter range - Ohm's law numerical
questions.question: Ramya wants to measure the current flowing through a circuit where a 12 V battery is connected to three resistors: R1 = 2 ohm in series with R2 = 8 ohm and R3 = 4 ohm connected in parallel with each other. Given four ammeters with ranges P (0-1 mA), Q (0-10 mA), R (0-1 A) and S (0-10 A), which ammeter should she use? Show your calculation.
